temperature, different time: thickness decides how long the heat takes to reach the middle. Size Air fryer Oven Small (51–60 per lb) 400°F / 205°C · 5 min 425°F / 220°C · 6 min Large (31–40 per lb) 400°F / 205°C · 7 min 425°F / 220°C · 9 min Jumbo (16–20 per lb) 400°F / 205°C · 9 min 425°F / 220°C · 11 min The one-minute window Shrimp cook in minutes and overcook in one. Their muscle tightens quickly in heat, so the gap between tender and rubbery is very short, and in an air fryer it is easy to miss while you are preparing the sauce. Size is the main variable, which is why shrimp are sold by count per pound: small shrimp can be done before jumbo ones have even turned pink. Cook one size at a time, set a timer for the shortest time in the table, and look at them rather than waiting for the end. The other common mistake is cooking shrimp that are still partly frozen, which leaves the outside tough and the centre underdone. Worked example A pound of large (31–40 count) shrimp, peeled, deveined and patted dry, tossed with a tablespoon of oil, garlic and paprika. Preheat for 4 minutes, spread them in one layer and cook at 400°F for 7 minutes, shaking once halfway. Small shrimp need about 5 minutes and jumbo shrimp about 9. On a tray in a conventional oven they take 425°F for around 9 minutes. How to tell they are done Look at the shape and colour. Raw shrimp are grey and translucent; cooked shrimp are pink-orange and opaque all the way through. A shrimp that has curled into a loose C is done, while a tight O means it has gone too far. The food-safety figure is 145°F (63°C), but shrimp are too small to measure easily; colour is the practical test. Take them out the moment the last grey patch disappears. Before they go in Thaw frozen shrimp completely, in the fridge overnight or in a bowl of cold water for about 20 minutes, then dry them well. Peeled shrimp cook more evenly than shell-on ones and take seasoning better. Add a little oil so the spices stick, and do not crowd the basket: a single layer cooks evenly, a heap steams. About 7 minutes at 400°F for large (31–40 count) shrimp, shaken once. Small shrimp take around 5 minutes and jumbo shrimp around 9. How do I know when air fryer shrimp are done? They turn pink and opaque and curl into a loose C shape. A tight O shape means they are overcooked. Can I cook frozen shrimp in the air fryer? It is better to thaw them first. Cooked from frozen, the outside toughens before the centre is done. Twenty minutes in cold water is enough. Do I need to shake shrimp in the air fryer? Once, halfway through, so the pieces underneath get the same colour as the ones on top. What is the oven equivalent for shrimp? 425°F for around 9 minutes on a tray in a conventional oven. mainEntity.name: How long does shrimp take in the air fryer?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 7 minutes at 400°F for large (31–40 count) shrimp, shaken once. Small shrimp take around 5 minutes and jumbo shrimp around 9.

mainEntity.name: How do I know when air fryer shrimp are done?

acceptedAnswer.text: They turn pink and opaque and curl into a loose C shape. A tight O shape means they are overcooked.

mainEntity.name: Can I cook frozen shrimp in the air fryer?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is better to thaw them first. Cooked from frozen, the outside toughens before the centre is done. Twenty minutes in cold water is enough.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to shake shrimp in the air fryer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Once, halfway through, so the pieces underneath get the same colour as the ones on top.

mainEntity.name: What is the oven equivalent for shrimp?

acceptedAnswer.text: 425°F for around 9 minutes on a tray in a conventional oven.
